title: Redwood Deep Dive - 128k+ Long Context Runtime
summary: Technical deep dive focused on long-context (128k+) performance: KV cache sizing and management, chunking/overlap strategies, attention optimizations (sparse/sliding/flash), batching tradeoffs, quantization options and impact, and private/VPC deployment constraints. Agreed to run a 128k benchmark pilot on customer data, share kernel-level telemetry, and follow up with pricing/commit proposal.
next_steps: Redwood: share 128k benchmark spreadsheet and runbook (link)
Customer: provide representative 128k prompt set and sample doc corpus
Schedule pilot run (2 weeks) and kernel-level telemetry collection
Follow-up meeting to review results and pricing proposal
action_items: Jordan Lee: send benchmark spreadsheet + security pack (due: 2025-08-18)
Maya Chen: upload sample 128k prompt set to secure bucket (due: 2025-08-21)
Priya Raman: prepare pilot config (model size, quantization levels, batching policy) and runbook (due: 2025-08-20)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Nina (Redwood Infra), Alex (CTO - Nimbus), Maya (Lead ML), Tom (Infra), Sana (Security)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, going to kick off real quick. agenda is deep dive on long-context runtime and our approach for 128k+ prompts. priya will drive tech stuff.
[00:18] Priya: hi all, quick note — we ran a couple of internal 128k runs last month; i'll share slides and the benchmark sheet. main things to cover: kv cache memory growth, chunking strategies, attention optimizations (sliding vs sparse), batching impact on latency, and quantization options.
[00:35] Alex: high level — we want to support full medical records bundles, often >100k tokens, and keep generation latency <10s for single-turn summarization. also must be air-gapped in some regions.
[00:52] Maya: and accuracy matters — we can't lose context when chunking. usual approach we use is 8k windows with retrieval but want a native 128k flow if possible.
[01:12] Priya: totally. two orthogonal pieces: memory/throughput (how KV scales) and model attention math (how compute scales). for KV: for transformer storage, the KV cache size scales linearly with sequence length and model dims. rough rule we use: expect ~0.6-1.2 bytes per token per layer per head depending on quantization/precision and implementation, so 128k is significant. for example, for a 70B model at fp16 we saw KV footprint around 70-120 GB for 128k, varies by layer count and head dims — this is why we often recommend sharding the KV cache across GPUs or using our dedicated instance types.
[02:05] Tom: can you clarify "sharding" — do you mean model parallel or KV sharding? hardware layout?
[02:12] Priya: good callout — two options: 1) model sharding (tensor/model parallel) which spreads both weights and KV across GPUs; 2) KV-only sharding where weights are replicated but KV cache is partitioned across devices. KV-shard lets you keep per-token latency lower for small batches but requires fast interconnect (nvlink/rdma).
[02:35] Nina: on infra side, we prefer KV-shard for the 128k use-case because it offloads memory pressure. we also support distributed KV with async fetching to reduce per-token blocking. there are tradeoffs: cross-GPU hops add ~1-2ms per hop depending on hw.
[02:55] [transcription glitch] Speaker 3: um the TV cache, no, sorry I mean KV cache — what about page faults on host memory?
[03:05] Priya: yeah occasionally on lower mem machines you'll see spill to host which kills latency. our private deployments avoid that by sizing VRAM or using NVMe-backed spill as a last resort with async prefetch to hide latency.
[03:20] Alex: for our compliance group, spill to disk is a non-starter unless it's encrypted and audited, so we need clear guarantees.
[03:30] Sana: SOC2 + support for HSM/KMS is mandatory; can you outline what Redwood Private provides?
[03:38] Jordan: Redwood Private includes customer-managed control plane, KMS integration, audit logs, and optional on-prem packaging. we'll send the security pack.
[03:45] Maya: back to chunking — what's your recommended strategy to maintain coherence across 128k while being efficient?
[03:55] Priya: we generally see two patterns: full-context native (single forward with KV up to 128k) or hierarchical/chunked approach. full-context gives best end-to-end coherence but costs more memory and compute. chunking strategies we recommend:
- chunk into 8k-16k windows with overlap (256-1024 tokens) plus a hierarchical summary layer (periodic compressed summaries)
- use retrieval-augmented generation: embed 4k chunks, retrieve top-k, stitch with marker tokens and short summary prompts
- sliding-window attention or sparse attention kernels for parts of the model — e.g., local attention for lower layers, global attention for higher layers

[04:45] Priya: an implementation we like is: ingest docs -> 4k chunks with 512 overlap -> build condensed summaries every N chunks -> for generation, have a two-phase pass: retrieve top relevant chunks + include last M tokens of live convo in KV. this often gets you near the quality of full 128k at a fraction of cost.
[05:05] Maya: how about attention optimizations — flash attention, aliBi, or sparse? what's in your runtime?
[05:12] Priya: runtime uses a kernel selection layer. we pick between flash attention (when memory fits and GPU supports it), Triton-optimized kernels, and sparse/sliding kernels. for 128k we often combine strategies: lower layers use local/sliding windows to keep compute O(n * w) while top layers have global attention on summary tokens. this hybrid reduces compute from O(n^2) to near-linear for most parts.
[05:45] Ethan: also note compiler-level optimizations matter — fused softmax, kernel fusion in attention, and memory-efficient KV packing improve end-to-end throughput.
[05:55] Alex: any ballpark numbers? if we go native 128k with a 70B model, what's generation time for a short summary (input 128k, output 512 tokens) under your Dedicated setup?
[06:08] Priya: ballpark from our internal runs: with H100s and KV-shard across 8 GPUs, quantized to 4-bit (q4_k_m), and aggressive kernel tuning, 128k->512 summary run is in the 6-12s range depending on beam/temperature. without sharding or on smaller GPUs it can be 20-40s. these are noisy numbers and depend on decode strategy and batching.
[06:38] Tom: and what's the token/sec throughput for streaming or batched requests?
[06:44] Priya: for batched generation on optimized hardware we see 5k-20k tokens/sec aggregate depending on model and quant; for single-request lowest-latency path it's much lower, maybe 200-1500 tokens/sec depending on precision.
[07:02] Maya: quantization — do you support q4/q2 and how does it affect quality for clinical text?
[07:10] Priya: we support q8, q4 variants (q4_k_m, q4_0, q4_x depending on model family) and some experimental q2 for smaller models. for clinical accuracy we usually recommend q4_k_m or fp16; q4_k_m gives ~8-12% speedup and small quality delta which we quantify in evals. we'll run regen tests on your prompt set.
[07:35] Alex: curious about memory numbers again — can you share typical KV memory for 16k vs 128k on a 70B?
[07:42] Priya: quick roughs: 16k might be ~8-16 GB KV footprint; 128k ramps to ~60-120 GB as earlier said, again varies. that's why for 128k we either rely on larger VRAM nodes (H100 80GB+ with model/KV sharding) or dedicated KV sharding across GPUs.
[08:02] Nina: we also offer compressed KV representations in Dedicated that trade a bit of compute to reduce memory by ~20-30% using block quantization for KV. that helps avoid spills.
[08:15] Tom: for on-prem can we pin GPUs and NVLink topology? we want predictable latency spikes.
[08:21] Nina: yes on-prem package includes topology recommendations and a layout guide. we can also do NUMA pinning and prewarm strategies to avoid page faults, and we provide startup scripts for hugepage/pinned memory.
[08:35] Maya: batching — if we batch multiple long-context requests, do we lose ability to stream partial outputs?
[08:42] Priya: batching improves overall throughput and unit cost but increases tail latency; for streaming we do micro-batching and autotrigger flush thresholds so you can get streaming while still benefiting partially from batching. for strict single-turn latency SLOs we recommend smaller micro-batches or dedicated single-tenant lanes.
[09:00] Alex: failure modes — what happens if one GPU in KV-sharded job fails mid-request?
[09:07] Priya: we have graceful fallback policies: replica fallback (if model weights replicated) or degrade to partial context (last N tokens) while we rehydrate KV, plus circuit-breaker to retry on another node. for critical workloads we recommend warm replicas.
[09:25] Maya: curious about your tracing/observability — can we get token-level timing and per-kernel traces?
[09:31] Ethan: Redwood Console exposes per-route token latency breakdowns, per-kernel timing, and we can enable more verbose kernel traces for pilots. we can also stream profiler logs for analysis.
[09:45] [15 minute mark - deeper technical q&a, skipped a few minute markers but transcript continues] 
[15:12] Maya: you mentioned hybrid attention (local + global). how do you pick which tokens get global attention?
[15:20] Priya: heuristics + learned selectors. simple rule: select summary tokens, question/answer markers, and entity-rich segments. we also support learned selector modules that mark global tokens during preprocessing.
[16:00] Tom: how much does network latency hurt when KV is remote across nodes?
[16:07] Priya: microseconds add up. a single cross-host hop can be 10-50us on good RDMA; with many layers it adds a few ms. for low-latency single-turns we prefer NVLink within node or tightly-coupled racks.
[16:25] Maya: for our compliance we need audit logs of prompts and KV access — is that supported?
[16:31] Jordan: yes audit logs capture request metadata; KV is ephemeral but we log access patterns and retention policies; for Private deployments we can integrate with your SIEM and KMS.
[16:45] Alex: okay let's talk pilot shape — what do you need from us?
[16:51] Priya: ideally: 1) representative prompt set (you said 128k examples) 2) a small corpus 1-2TB to simulate (or subset) 3) target SLOs and quality metrics 4) allowed quant levels and infra constraints. we'll run three configs: native 128k fp16 on Dedicated, q4_k_m KV-shard hybrid, and chunked/hierarchical retrieval baseline.
[17:18] Maya: timeline?
[17:20] Jordan: we can start the pilot as soon as we have datasets and VPC connectivity. typical pilot runs 1-2 weeks of testing plus 1 week for analysis.
[17:30] [noise/overlap] Customer (Tom): we'll need details for VPC peering and our security team needs the SOC2 docs.
[17:36] Jordan: will send security pack and runbook today.
[17:40] Priya: a couple of extra notes from internal perf runs: using flash attention plus q4_k_m we saw 20-35% speedups on H100 for long-context compared to fp16 in some models, but some edge-case tokenization patterns worsen for quant; so regen evals matter. also note memory fragmentation (CUDA allocator) can create spikes — we mitigate with reserved pooling and prewarming.
[18:10] Maya: do you support on-the-fly chunk recombination? e.g., stream back intermediate summaries then re-embed on the fly?
[18:17] Priya: yes that's supported in our runtime flow: you can do staged decoding where intermediate summaries are merged into context and re-encoded. it's slower but gives the best of retrieval + context.
[18:35] Alex: cost — any back-of-envelope on compute cost delta between native 128k vs chunked pipeline?
[18:42] Jordan: ballpark: native 128k can be 3-8x more expensive per request compared to a well-tuned chunked + retrieval pipeline because of O(n^2) compute in some attention implementations; with our optimizations that gap narrows. dedicated commitments and batching help amortize cost.
[19:05] [mid call, customer asks about specific models]
[19:10] Maya: what about open models vs your curated variants — do you recommend a smaller model with retrieval vs large model native 128k?
[19:18] Priya: often retrieval + smaller 13B/34B model with good prompting can match or beat 70B native for many tasks with huge cost savings. but for nuanced clinical reasoning larger models still have an edge. pilot should include a couple model families.
[19:35] Alex: Jenkins question — can we run this in our air-gapped cluster?
[19:39] Nina: yes on-prem package supports air-gapped deployment; we provide install containers, offline license, and KMS integration via HSM appliance.
[19:50] Maya: any gotchas for quantization on on-prem GPUs?
[19:55] Priya: older GPUs without tensor cores see less benefit from q4; tuning and kernel availability matter. we have fallback kernels but perf delta is smaller on older hw.
[20:10] [long section of bench discussion — highlights only]
[20:25] Priya: plan for the pilot: we'll run three experiments and collect metrics: latency P50/P95/P99, throughput, memory footprint, repro/regen quality scores, and token-level kernel traces. we'll share the benchmark sheet and a short automated script to run locally in your env.
[20:48] Maya: will you also share the tradeoff dashboard so we can compare cost vs quality?
[20:53] Ethan: yes Redwood Console has a dashboard; we'll provide a pilot view and a shared spreadsheet.
[21:05] Alex: good. who owns the pilot orchestration?
[21:09] Jordan: Redwood AE/SE pair will manage orchestration with your infra lead (Tom).
[21:15] Tom: Tom here — we'll need an IP allowlist and test VPC peering info.
[21:20] Jordan: noted.
[21:25] [40 minute mark - deeper infra subtleties]
[40:02] Priya: additional notes: for kernel selection we look at sequence length distribution. if 99% of requests are <=16k but occasional 128k spikes, we recommend a hybrid routing policy: route small requests to single-GPU low-latency nodes and route rare 128k requests to KV-sharded heavy nodes. this avoids constant overprovisioning.
[40:30] Maya: what about caching prefixes — can we reuse KV across similar prompts?
[40:36] Priya: yes prefix/KV caching is a big win. if prompts share initial doc context we can keep KV warm and serve subsequent requests at much lower cost. Redwood supports prefix cache invalidation policies.
[40:50] Alex: data residency — we need EU-only for some records. is regional routing supported?
[40:56] Jordan: yes region routing and data residency controls are part of Redwood Dedicated/Private. we'll note that in the follow-up security doc.
[41:10] [50 minute mark - wrap up]
[50:05] Jordan: recap: Redwood to send benchmark sheet and security pack; customer to provide sample prompts and confirm infra contacts; pilot to run three configs; follow-up meeting in ~2 weeks to review.
[50:20] Maya: one more item — can you include example config for hybrid attention?
[50:25] Priya: yes will include config/ops knobs: layer split, window sizes, overlap, selector thresholds.
[50:33] Alex: thanks all. anything else?
[50:36] Sana: please include compliance contacts and evidence of SOC2 + ISO in the pack.
[50:40] Jordan: will do.
[50:45] [end call admin chatter and scheduling]

Notes/Artifacts referenced: benchmark spreadsheet link: https://redwood-internal.example/benchmarks/128k-pilot-2025.xlsx (shared), security pack: link to docs (sent after meeting), sample kernel traces (available on request).

End of transcript.
notes: Artifacts: 128k benchmark spreadsheet (link above), pilot runbook, security pack. Agreed configurations: native 128k fp16; q4_k_m KV-shard hybrid; chunked retrieval baseline. Priorities: avoid disk spill, ensure KMS/HSM integration, and collect token-level kernel traces.
